Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Power Holdings Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Power Holdings' Q3 2024 Earnings Call. Joining me on the call today are John Ramirez, Chief Executive Officer; Elena Vasquez, Chief Financial Officer; Mike Chen, Chief Operating Officer, and Lisa Patel, Chief Strategy Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that statements made during this call that are not historical facts are forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our SEC filings for a detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'll turn the call over to John Ramirez.

John Ramirez: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on our performance this quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities, delivering solid results in a challenging environment.

Our performance was driven by:
    1. Strong updates on regulatory rate case filings and outcomes.
    2. Excellent reliability metrics including SAIDI and SAIFI, alongside superior system performance.
    3. Significant progress towards our clean energy goals and emission reductions.
    4. Financial results that exceeded our guidance.
    5. Clear earnings guidance for the next quarter and full year.

Let me provide some more detail on these five key aspects. Elena, please start us off with the regulatory updates.

Elena Vasquez: Good morning, everyone. As we continue to execute on our $15 billion five-year capital plan focused on grid resilience, clean energy transition, and customer affordability, regulatory updates remain a cornerstone of our story at Apex Power Holdings. Today, I'll provide a detailed overview of our recent rate case filings and outcomes across our six-state footprint—primarily in the PJM and MISO footprints, with exposure to ERCOT and CAISO borders. These proceedings are critical for recovering our investments in high-voltage transmission upgrades, 2 GW of near-term battery storage additions, and advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) rollouts, all while aligning with FERC Order 1000 competitive transmission processes and state-level IRPs mandating 80% carbon-free generation by 2035.

Let me start with our most recent activity. In Pennsylvania, where we serve 1.2 million customers through our subsidiary PennPower Utilities, we filed a full rate case with the Pennsylvania PUC in late Q2, requesting a $285 million annual revenue increase on a $4.2 billion rate base. This filing reflects a 9.75% ROE request at a 52% equity ratio, incorporating $450 million in CWIP for our Susquehanna Valley 500 kV transmission line— a key interconnector enhancing PJM locational marginal pricing (LMP) stability amid growing data center load from hyperscalers like Amazon Web Services. We also sought recovery for $120 million in post-in-service carrying costs (PISC) related to our completed AMI deployment, which now covers 95% of our PA meters and has driven a 15% reduction in non-technical losses through real-time outage detection.

The PUC issued a final order last week, authorizing $240 million—84% of our ask—effective October 1st. While we saw a modest trim on ROE to 9.5%, the settlement preserved full CWIP recovery and included a multi-year rate plan (MYRP) mechanism for the next three years, allowing formulaic adjustments tied to 90-day Treasury yields plus a 650 bps equity risk premium. This outcome translates to a 12 bps positive EPS impact in 2024 and supports 4-6% regulated earnings growth annually. Notably, customer bills rise only 4.2% on average, below the state decoupling threshold, thanks to our energy efficiency programs that shaved 2.5% off weather-normalized usage last year.

Shifting to the Midwest, our Ohio operations under Buckeye Power filed a distribution rate case with the PUCO in April, seeking $180 million on a $2.8 billion rate base. Key drivers included $300 million in capex for substation automation and DERMS (Distributed Energy Resource Management Systems) to integrate 500 MW of customer-sited solar under Ohio's net metering revisions. We requested a 10.25% ROE at 53% equity, factoring in heightened wildfire risk modeling per FERC's Risk-Informed Decision Analysis (RIDA) guidelines—Ohio's seen a 30% uptick in extreme weather events per NOAA data.

PUCO approved a settlement in early September for $155 million—86% recovery—with ROE at 9.75% and inclusion of a forward-looking tracker for EV charger incentives, unlocking $50 million in IRA Section 30C tax credits. This is our third consecutive Ohio rate case with over 80% recovery, reflecting strong stakeholder alignment. Financially, it adds 8 bps to EPS this year and positions us to earn our authorized ROE on 98% of our Ohio rate base by year-end, up from 92% last quarter. Regionally, this supports our strategic pivot toward VPPs (Virtual Power Plants), aggregating 100 MW of battery-backed residential solar for MISO capacity auctions, where we cleared at $150/kW-month premiums.

In Texas, our ERCOT-focused generation arm, Lone Star GenCo, pursued a hybrid rate case/GT&C (Generator Tariff and Cost) proceeding with the PUCT. Filed in Q1, we requested $210 million in transmission cost recovery for our 1.2 GW Corpus Christi Wind Farm interconnection upgrades, including $75 million for synchronous condensers to mitigate inverter-based resource (IBR) stability risks—critical as ERCOT's IBR penetration hit 45% this summer. ROE ask was 10.5% at 55% equity, benchmarked against peers like NextEra's 10.2% in recent FERC filings.

The outcome was favorable: PUCT authorized $195 million in late August, with full formula rate treatment and a performance incentive adder of 50 bps for meeting 99.9% reliability during Heat Wave 2024. This not only recovers our $1.1 billion rate base but accelerates depreciation on legacy coal assets, aligning with Texas' SB7 renewables mandate. EPS accretion is 10 bps for 2024, with upside from ancillary services revenue, which surged 25% YoY to $45 million on black start capabilities.

We've also seen constructive developments in pending dockets. Our Virginia rate case—filed June 30th with the SCC for $320 million on a $5.1 billion rate base—remains on track for a Q1 2025 order. It incorporates $600 million CWIP for Dominion-partnered offshore wind transmission ties and seeks 9.8% ROE amid PJM's RTEP (Regional Transmission Expansion Plan) Cycle 2024 approvals. Early evidentiary hearings suggest 85%+ recovery potential, bolstered by our alignment with Virginia's 100% clean energy by 2050 VCEA goals. Similarly, in West Virginia, our PSC docket for $95 million (grid hardening post-Hurricane Helene analogs) is in settlement phase, with management expecting closure by December at 9.25% ROE.

Broader trends and strategic insights: Across our portfolio, rate case recovery ratios averaged 85% this year, up from 78% in 2023, driven by PUCs' increasing recognition of capex imperatives under the IRA's $370 billion clean energy incentives. We've secured $450 million in PTC/ITC transfers to date, with rate base growth projected at 7% CAGR through 2028. Equity ratios stabilized at 52-55%, despite FERC's single-issue ratemaking scrutiny in Coakley v. BJ Energy. Wildfire mitigation funds—$200 million authorized across states—mirror PG&E/Cal ISO precedents, with our dynamic line rating (DLR) pilots boosting transfer capacity 15% without new wires.

Looking ahead, we're proactively filing two MYRPs in 2025: Pennsylvania Phase II ($350M) and Ohio ($220M), embedding trackers for hydrogen blending pilots and CCUS (Carbon Capture Utilization Storage) readiness per DOE's 45Q credits. These position us for 5-7% EPS growth, with ROE equity at 10% by 2026. Risks include potential DCNPP (Deferred Costs Not Previously Passed) challenges in Ohio and PUCT's weather normalization disputes, but our 2.5x interest coverage and BBB+ ratings provide ample buffer.

In summary, these rate outcomes affirm our disciplined regulatory strategy, funding $3.2 billion in 2024 capex while keeping bills affordable—average residential increase of 3.8% vs. 5.2% national utility peer average per EEI data. We're not just recovering costs; we're building a resilient, decarbonized grid for the AI/data center boom.

John Ramirez: Thank you, Elena, for that comprehensive update on our regulatory progress—truly a testament to our proactive approach. Mike, over to you for details on our reliability metrics and system performance.

Mike Chen: Good morning, everyone. I'll dive right into our reliability metrics and system performance, as this remains a cornerstone of our value proposition at Apex Power Holdings. As you know, in the utilities sector, reliability isn't just a regulatory checkbox—it's directly tied to customer satisfaction, regulatory ROE multipliers under frameworks like those from FERC and state commissions, and our ability to justify capex recoveries in rate cases. We're reporting on our key IEEE 1366 metrics: SAIDI, the System Average Interruption Duration Index, and SAIFI, the System Average Interruption Frequency Index. These exclude major events like the Category 4 derecho we saw in Iowa last summer, per NERC standards, to focus on controllable performance.

For full-year 2023, I'm pleased to report our ex-ante SAIDI came in at 82.4 customer-minutes per year— that's a 14% improvement year-over-year from 95.7 minutes in 2022, and well below the national median of 104 minutes reported by the EIA's latest Form 861 data. Our Midwest peer group, including the likes of Alliant Energy and Ameren, averaged around 98 minutes, so we're punching above our weight. SAIFI clocked in at 1.15 system average interruptions per customer, down 12% from 1.31 in 2022 and ahead of the peer median of 1.28. These gains held steady even as we integrated 15% more renewables onto our grid, with wind capacity from our partnerships with NextEra and Invenergy pushing DER penetration to 22% of peak load.

Breaking it down regionally, our Northern Division—covering Minnesota and Wisconsin—led the pack with a stellar SAIDI of 68.2 minutes, thanks to proactive storm hardening post-2021's polar vortex remnants. That's 20% better than 2022 and beats Xcel Energy's regional benchmarks by 8%. The challenge was our Central Division in Illinois and Iowa, where SAIDI ticked up to 92.1 minutes due to a series of micro-outages from aging infrastructure—think 60-year-old wood poles stressed by wet bulb temperatures exceeding 28°C during July heat waves. But even there, SAIFI improved to 1.22 from 1.45, reflecting our vegetation management program's success: we trimmed or removed 45,000 trees this year, a 25% increase via LiDAR-enabled drone surveys from Trimble Navigation tech.

Quarterly trends underscore our momentum. Q4 SAIDI was a banner 18.6 minutes ex-weather—our best ever—versus 22.4 in Q4 2022. This was driven by the rollout of our $150 million Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS) from GE Grid Solutions, which uses real-time analytics to isolate faults 40% faster. Fault location accuracy hit 96%, reducing CAIDI—our Customer Average Interruption Duration—to just 71 minutes per event. Comparatively, PG&E's post-wildfire investments have them targeting sub-100 SAIDI, but we're already there without California's unique fire risks.

What fueled these improvements? First, our $450 million grid modernization capex bucket, up 18% YoY, prioritized high-impact initiatives. We replaced 12,000 poles with composite fiberglass from Strongwell, targeting high-failure circuits identified via our Synergi Electric modeler from DNV. Undergrounding 120 miles of overhead lines in urban corridors—like Chicago's South Side—cut weather-related outages by 35%. On the tech front, our pilot of ABB's Ability Predictive Analytics platform, powered by machine learning on 50,000 PMUs (Phasor Measurement Units), flagged 85% of potential vegetation encroachments before failure, saving an estimated $12 million in O&M.

Predictive maintenance deserves a spotlight: partnering with Siemens Energy, we deployed digital twins for our 500 kV transmission fleet, simulating extreme events like the Texas 2021 freeze analog. This reduced forced outage rates by 22%, aligning us with top-quartile NERC BAL standards. EV integration is another tailwind—we've hardened 200 substations for bidirectional flow under our VPP program with GM and Ford, accommodating 50,000 new Level 2 chargers without spiking SAIFI.

Regionally, the Midwest's weather volatility—2023 saw 15% more severe storms than the 10-year average per NOAA—tested us, but our investments paid off. In contrast to ERCOT's ongoing grid stress from renewables intermittency, our diversified fleet (45% gas, 30% nuclear from our Quad Cities plant, 25% renewables) maintained 99.97% availability. Customer impact? Our CSI score hit 78/100, up from 72, correlating directly to a 2.5% revenue uplift via Illinois Commerce Commission performance incentives.

Strategically, these metrics de-risk our $2.8 billion five-year capex plan, filed last month with MISO and state regulators. We're targeting SAIDI under 75 minutes and SAIFI below 1.10 by 2025, unlocking up to 50 bps in ROE adders—similar to Duke Energy's Carolina success. This supports 6-8% EPS growth through efficient capex recovery, with IRR on reliability projects averaging 11%. Risks? Rising cyber threats—we're investing $40 million in IEC 61850-compliant defenses—and supply chain snarls for transformers, but our stockpiles mitigate that.

In sum, our reliability edge positions Apex Power Holdings as a resilient operator in a decarbonizing world, where CAISO-like curtailments from poor grid performance are non-starters.

John Ramirez: Outstanding work on reliability, Mike—it's a key differentiator for us. Lisa, please share our progress on clean energy goals and emission reductions.

Lisa Patel: Thank you, John, and good morning, everyone. As we report another strong quarter with adjusted EPS of $1.42, up 8% year-over-year, I'd like to dive into our sustainability pillar, which is not just an ESG checkbox but a core driver of long-term value creation in the Utilities sector. At Apex Power Holdings, we're accelerating our transition to a cleaner, more resilient energy mix amid surging demand from electrification, data centers, and AI hyperscalers. Let me walk you through our FY2024 progress, key initiatives, regional dynamics, and how this positions us for superior risk-adjusted returns.

First, on emissions: We've achieved a 28% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions year-over-year, bringing us to 42 million metric tons of CO2e—well ahead of our 2030 target of 50% below our 2019 baseline of 75 million metric tons. This marks the steepest annual drop since our 2021 coal retirements kicked in. Scope 3 emissions from upstream fuel supply have dipped 12% thanks to our shift away from high-GHG coal contracts, now comprising just 15% of our generation stack versus 32% three years ago. These reductions are verified by our third-party auditor, similar to the SBTi-aligned protocols used by peers like NextEra Energy.

Driving this is our renewables buildout. We've commissioned 1.8 GW of new clean capacity YTD, including 1.2 GW of utility-scale solar—our largest vintage ever—leveraging the Inflation Reduction Act's uncapped ITC at 30% plus the energy community adder, which boosted our after-tax yield to 9.5%. Highlights include the 450 MW SunForge Solar project in Texas' ERCOT market, utilizing high-efficiency bifacial PERC modules from First Solar, achieving a capacity factor of 28%—10% above zonal averages due to single-axis trackers and our proprietary AI-optimized O&M platform. We've also locked in 15-year PPAs with tech giants like Google and Microsoft at $35-40/MWh, hedging LCOE risks in a market where spot solar PPAs are trading at $25/MWh in sunny ISOs.

Wind remains a cornerstone: 600 MW added, headlined by the 300 MW Apex Breeze offshore project off the Carolinas, mirroring Vineyard Wind's success but with GE Haliade-X turbines at 13 MW each. This facility hit 95% availability in its first full quarter, with levelized costs now competitive at $50/MWh post-ITC. Our total renewables portfolio now stands at 12.5 GW, or 48% of our 26 GW rate base—up from 35% in 2022—positioning us as a top-5 U.S. renewable owner-operator, neck-and-neck with Ørsted and Dominion Energy.

Battery storage is our grid resilience play. We've deployed 1.4 GWh across four sites, including a landmark 500 MWh, four-hour BESS at our Texas hub, co-located with solar for hybrid dispatch. Partnering with Tesla's Megapack and Fluence's Gridstack, we're arbitraging ERCOT's volatility—capturing $150/kW-year in ancillary services revenue—while enabling 20% more solar curtailment avoidance. This supports our clean energy goals by firming intermittency; our portfolio-wide storage attachment rate is now 25% on new renewables.

Regionally, progress varies but is robust. In the Southeast (Southeastern PJM and SERC), where coal still lingers at 18% of the mix industry-wide, we've retired two 600 MW subcritical coal units at our legacy Riverbend plant, repowering with a 50/50 gas-CCUS blend using Mitsubishi's Advanced KM CDR process, capturing 90% of CO2 for EOR sales. This slashed site emissions 65% while preserving baseload reliability amid Vogtle-like nuclear delays. Southeast renewables penetration hit 22% in our territory, fueled by state RPS mandates in Georgia and the Carolinas.

Texas ERCOT is our growth engine: Renewables now 55% of our dispatchable capacity here, up from 40%, riding the state's 50 GW renewable boom. Despite curtailments peaking at 2.5 TWh last summer, our storage and demand response curtailed losses to under 1%, and we're eyeing hydrogen blending pilots with Cheniere Energy to decarbonize our 2 GW gas fleet.

Northeast (ISO-NE and NYISO) sees offshore wind as the unlock: Our 1.2 GW pipeline secured BOEM approvals, tapping into CLCPA-funded contracts at $100/MWh all-in. Challenges like supply chain bottlenecks from Siemens Gamesa delays pushed CODs to 2026, but we're mitigating with domestic content bonuses under IRA Section 45X.

Strategically, we're optimizing our thermal fleet for the 2030s. Our integrated resource plan retires another 1.5 GW coal by 2026, offset by 2 GW CCGT with post-combustion CCS readiness, targeting 95% capture rates akin to NRG's Petra Nova revival. We're also pioneering green hydrogen: A 100 MW electrolyzer at our California site, fed by excess solar, produces 10,000 tons/year for peaker blending—partnered with Plug Power under a 10-year offtake.

Market tailwinds are immense: U.S. power demand growth revised to 4.7% CAGR through 2028 by EIA, driven by 100 GW data center load by 2030. IRA transferability lets us monetize tax credits via financing partners like JPMorgan, de-risking $3.2 billion in FY25 capex at 8-10% ROE hurdles. REC markets remain liquid; we've banked 5 million MWh equivalents for compliance sales at $10-15/REC.

Looking ahead, we're on track for 60% clean energy by 2027 and net-zero Scope 1&2 by 2040, with carbon-neutral Scope 3 via supplier engagements. This isn't altruism—it's alpha generation: Our clean assets trade at 12x forward EBITDA versus 9x for thermal peers, and we've seen a 15% TSR premium YTD. Risks like interest rate sensitivity on long-dated projects are hedged via 70% fixed-rate debt at 4.2%, and supply chain inflation is capped through frame agreements.

In summary, our clean energy momentum is translating to resilient earnings: $200 million in avoided fuel costs this year alone, plus $150 million in PTC/ITC cash flows. We're not just meeting goals—we're exceeding them, creating shareholder value in a decarbonizing world.

John Ramirez: Thank you, Lisa—that progress really sets us apart. Now, Elena, back to you to cover our financial performance relative to guidance.

Elena Vasquez: Good morning, everyone. I'll now provide an overview of our financial performance relative to the guidance we outlined during our Q2 call for Apex Power Holdings. Overall, we delivered a strong quarter, significantly exceeding our guidance across key metrics, driven by robust load growth from data centers and industrial electrification, higher-than-expected renewable dispatch, and favorable capacity auction outcomes in key ISO markets. Let me break this down in detail.

Starting with the top line: We reported consolidated revenues of $2.85 billion, up 12% year-over-year and beating our guidance midpoint of $2.65 billion by approximately 8%. This outperformance was primarily fueled by our Regulated Utilities segment, which generated $1.92 billion in revenues—$150 million ahead of our guided range of $1.75 billion to $1.80 billion. Key drivers here included weather-normalized retail sales growth of 4.2%, outpacing our 3% forecast, thanks to sustained demand from hyperscale data centers in our Texas and PJM footprints. For context, ERCOT load growth hit 15% YoY in Q3, with our assets capturing meaningful upside from real-time pricing spikes during peak summer hours.

Our Competitive Power Generation segment also contributed strongly, posting $820 million in revenues versus our $750 million to $770 million guidance. This reflects 92% average hedge coverage at attractive economics—our gas-fired fleet achieved a 68% capacity factor, bolstered by $45 million in positive spark spreads from Henry Hub prices averaging $3.25/MMBtu, 15% above our hedge assumptions. Additionally, our renewables portfolio punched above its weight, with 2.8 million MWh generated, up 25% YoY and exceeding our 2.5 million MWh guide. This was driven by favorable wind resource yields in our Midwest assets (akin to NextEra's strong Iowa performance) and the full-quarter ramp of our 300 MW solar-plus-storage hybrid in California, which benefited from early PTC eligibility under the Inflation Reduction Act.

On the bottom line, adjusted EBITDA came in at $1.12 billion, smashing our $975 million to $1.025 billion guidance by 12%. Excluding one-offs like $20 million in favorable MISO capacity auction settlements, core EBITDA growth was still 9% YoY. Margins expanded to 39.4% from 37.2% last year, reflecting disciplined O&M cost management—our controllable O&M per MWh held flat at $18 despite inflationary pressures—and lower-than-guided fuel costs in our combined-cycle units.

GAAP net income was $425 million, or $0.92 per diluted share, but our headline adjusted EPS of $1.72 decisively beat our $1.50 to $1.60 guidance range by 14% at the midpoint. This marks our eighth straight quarter of EPS beats, underscoring the earnings power of our diversified fleet: 45% renewables, 35% gas, 15% nuclear, and 5% coal transition assets. Free cash flow before growth capex was $650 million, $75 million ahead of guidance, supporting our $0.78 quarterly dividend—up 5% YoY—and $300 million in share repurchases.

Regionally, performance was mixed but net positive. In the Northeast (PJM and ISO-NE), we overdelivered by 10% on EBITDA guidance, with our Susquehanna nuclear plant running at a 93% capacity factor and securing BRA auction clears at $240/MW-day—well above marginal costs. Texas (ERCOT) was a standout, contributing 22% EBITDA growth from battery storage arbitrage during heatwaves, mirroring patterns seen at peers like Vistra. However, our California utilities faced $30 million in headwinds from PG&E wildfire cost-sharing and CPUC-mandated rooftop solar compensation reductions, partially offsetting gains but still delivering in-line results.

Strategically, these results validate our 'Reliable Renewables' initiative: We've now brought 1.2 GW of new clean capacity online YTD, including four BESS projects totaling 800 MW/3,200 MWh, positioned for ERCOT's booming AI-driven loads. Our $4.2 billion 2024 capex plan—65% growth-oriented—remains on track, with AFUDC accretion of $55 million in Q3 boosting regulated ROE to 10.4%. Looking ahead, we're raising our full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $6.75-$6.95 from $6.50-$6.80, incorporating 2-3% higher load growth forecasts from EIA data center projections and $100 million in incremental IRA tax credits.

Challenges persist—nuclear uprates delayed by NRC inspections cost us $15 million, and rising interest expenses from our $12 billion debt stack (average cost 4.1%) pressured interest coverage to 5.2x. But our 75% investment-grade balance sheet, with $2.5 billion in liquidity, positions us well for pending rate cases in three states targeting 9.5-10% ROE.

In summary, Q3 demonstrates the resilience of our integrated model amid energy transition tailwinds.

John Ramirez: Excellent overview, Elena. And while you're on guidance, could you elaborate on our outlook for the next quarter and full year?

Elena Vasquez: Certainly, John. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for the question on forward guidance. As we turn to our outlook, I'm pleased to reaffirm our full-year view while providing a refined range for the back half, reflecting the continued strength in our regulated and contracted asset base, robust load growth from hyperscale data centers, and the early benefits from our renewables queue acceleration under the Inflation Reduction Act. Let me walk you through the details.

For Q4 2024 Guidance

For the fourth quarter, we expect adjusted earnings per share in the range of $1.28 to $1.38, representing about 5% year-over-year growth at the midpoint. This compares to our Q4 2023 adjusted EPS of $1.25 and reflects several tailwinds partially offset by seasonal dynamics.

On the top line, we anticipate consolidated revenues of $2.85 billion to $3.05 billion, up from $2.72 billion last year, driven by:
- 7% organic load growth in our Northeast and Midwest footprints, fueled by data center PPAs with colocation providers like Digital Realty and Equinix. ERCOT wholesale prices remain supportive, with our gas-fired peakers capturing $45/MWh average spark spreads during peak hours.
- Higher contributions from our renewables portfolio, where solar curtailment in CAISO has eased post our 150 MW battery co-location upgrades at our Desert Sun project, boosting capture rates to 92% from 85% YoY.

Adjusted EBITDA is guided at $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion, with margins holding steady at 37% to 38%. Key drivers include:
- Favorable weather normalization – Q4 HDDs projected at 10% above normal in PJM, supporting heating demand without the extremes we saw in prior quarters.
- Lower O&M costs from our $50 million fleet-wide digital twin initiative on our GE 7HA CCGTs, which has improved heat rate efficiency by 2.5% through predictive maintenance via Siemens MindSphere platform.

Offsetting factors include modestly higher natural gas costs – Henry Hub futures at $2.90/MMBtu – though our 85% hedged position through year-end at $2.60/MMBtu mitigates this. We also face $20 million in one-time regulatory disallowances from FERC's ROE review in MISO, but this is already baked into our regulated rate base growth of 4.2%.

Full-Year 2024 Guidance

Looking at the full year, we are narrowing and raising our adjusted EPS guidance to $5.25 to $5.45, up from our prior range of $5.10 to $5.40 and above consensus of $5.28. This implies 8% growth over 2023's $4.92, with the midpoint delivering $5.35 or a 9% increase.

Revenues are now expected at $11.6 billion to $12.0 billion, lifted by:
- $400 million incremental contribution from our 1.2 GW renewables pipeline, including the COD of our 400 MW Victory Wind Farm in SPP (backed by a 15-year PPA with Google) and the 300 MW Horizon Solar + Storage hybrid in ERCOT.
- Regulated electric delivery growth of 6%, driven by capex deployment of $2.1 billion – 60% on grid hardening and T&D resiliency post-2023's Hurricane Idalia impacts in the Southeast.

Adjusted EBITDA guidance tightens to $4.45 billion to $4.65 billion, with 40.5% margins at the midpoint. Highlights include:
- Nuclear uprate success: Our Palisades Unit 1 restart (modeled after Holtec's Michigan project) adds 50 MW of baseload capacity, with a 12% capacity factor uplift from advanced fuel assemblies.
- Renewables tailwinds: PTC/ITC extensions under IRA yielding $250 million in tax credits, plus our first-mover advantage in long-duration energy storage (LDES) with Form Energy's iron-air batteries at 100 MW/10-hour scale in PJM, qualifying for the full ITC adder.

Strategic offsets: Coal retirements at our Midwest basin plants complete by year-end, with replacement gas-to-renewables conversions maintaining 98% availability. Capex guidance holds at $2.4 billion to $2.6 billion, with 85% FCF conversion supporting our 4.1% dividend yield and $500 million share repurchase authorization.

Key Trends and Regional Insights

Demand remains our brightest spot: U.S. power consumption is tracking 3.5% YoY growth, but our exposure to high-growth regions amplifies this to 6-8%. In PJM, our 15 GW portfolio benefited from the BRA 2025/2026 auction clearing at $269.87/MW-day – 2x prior years – securing $300 million in net revenues. ERCOT continues to shine with real-time prices averaging $35/MWh YTD, our battery fleet arbitraging 20% of intervals profitably.

Conversely, CAISO faces headwinds from rooftop solar saturation (now 18 GW behind-the-meter), compressing midday prices, though our storage dispatch has captured $15 million in ancillary services. Weather outlook is benign: NOAA's Q4 forecast shows 5% above-normal temperatures in Texas, supporting cooling loads without drought-driven hydro constraints.

Strategic Outlook

We're laser-focused on the energy transition: Our IDG 2030 plan targets 60% carbon-free generation by decade-end, blending nuclear (20 GW pipeline via SMR partnerships with NuScale), offshore wind (500 MW from our Ørsted JV off New Jersey), and hydrogen-ready turbines with GE Vernova – blending up to 30% green H2 by 2027.

M&A remains opportunistic: Post our $1.2 billion acquisition of NextEra's Midwest solar assets, we're eyeing $2-3 billion in bolt-ons, funded by ATM equity and green bonds at 4.8% yields. Risks include supply chain delays on HVDC transmission (e.g., Siemens Energy transformer lead times) and policy shifts, but our 90% contracted backlog through 2030 de-risks execution.

In summary, our guidance reflects a resilient, growth-oriented platform poised to outperform in this electrification megatrend.

John Ramirez: Thank you, Elena, Mike, and Lisa for those in-depth insights—they really highlight the strength across our operations. To wrap up the prepared remarks, our capital expenditure for the quarter was $850 million, primarily focused on grid modernization and renewable integrations. We remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning value to shareholders through our dividend and buyback programs. Now, I'll turn the call over to Mike for a quick operational update, then Lisa on strategy before we open for questions.

Mike Chen: Thank you, John. On the operational front, we are seeing improved efficiency in our combined-cycle gas turbine power plants due to the implementation of advanced distribution management systems. This has resulted in a 15% increase in output while enhancing grid stability.

Lisa Patel: Thank you, Mike. Turning to our long-term strategy, we are actively exploring opportunities in the long-duration energy storage space. We believe this will be a key driver of future growth, complementing our clean energy advancements.

John Ramirez: Thank you, team. In summary, we delivered solid results in the Q3, demonstrating the strength of our business model, successful integration of Lone Star GenCo, and our commitment to creating long-term value for our shareholders. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and positioning Apex Power Holdings for continued success. Now, we'll open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

John Smith: Good morning, team. Can you elaborate on your plans for capex allocation in 2025?

John Ramirez: Certainly, John. Our $4.2 billion plan for next year prioritizes grid resilience and clean energy, with about 60% allocated to renewables and storage expansions, ensuring we capture data center growth while maintaining reliability.

Operator: Our next question comes from Sarah Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Sarah Lee: What is your outlook for the regulatory environment heading into 2025?

Elena Vasquez: Great question, Sarah. With our strong track record of 85% recovery rates and upcoming MYRPs in key states, we expect continued constructive outcomes, supporting 5-7% EPS growth as we embed new trackers for emerging tech like hydrogen and CCUS.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Kim with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

David Kim: How are you mitigating risks related to supply chain disruptions?

Mike Chen: Thanks, David. We've built strategic stockpiles for critical components like transformers, partnered with reliable suppliers like Siemens and GE for frame agreements, and leveraged digital twins for better forecasting—keeping our projects on track despite global pressures.
